preamble: Nine clues lack a definition; their solutions are of a kind.

clue.text: See 25
Religious symbol in art makes one good (before undies loosened)

parts.note: one as the indefinite article

indicators.note: clothing that has been loosened has come out of its proper shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sacred image in a painting is somehow tied to good behaviour and slack underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The Agnus Dei, Latin for Lamb of God, is shown in Christian art as a lamb carrying a cross or banner.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lamb of God is a standard emblem of Christ in paintings, stained glass and heraldry.

clue.text: Way over length in colour

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, enclosed by the outer letters

parts.note: a hue is a colour

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing placed over another comes before it in reading order

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
L is the abbreviation for length

explanation.surface: A route marked out a bit long on a map, coloured in.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the nine clues with no definition: the preamble's common kind is dances.
explanation.definitionFit: The hustle is a 1970s disco dance done in lines or pairs, so it belongs to the preamble's shared category.

clue.text: Non-vocal boxing fix

indicators.note: to box something is to pack it inside a container, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: mute means making no vocal sound
to set is to fix in place

explanation.surface: A silent fighter's bout has been rigged.
explanation.walkthrough: No definition here: the answer is one of the preamble's set.
explanation.definitionFit: A musette is an old French pastoral dance named after a small bagpipe, fitting the preamble's shared category.

clue.text: Disconnect the supply of international body publicity

parts.note: the UN, the United Nations
a plug is a piece of publicity for a product

explanation.surface: Someone cuts off the publicity machine of an international organisation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' suggests goods, but the definition is about cutting off electrical power to a device.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulling a plug from the socket cuts the electricity feeding an appliance.

clue.text: Birches surrounding new festival resort

indicators.note: surrounding something means forming a ring round it, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: birches and canes are both rods for corporal punishment
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Trees ring a newly opened holiday town hosting a festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Birches' reads as trees, but here it means the rods once used for beating, as do canes.
explanation.definitionFit: The French Riviera town is famous as the seaside host of the annual international film festival.

clue.text: Suitable prisoner, so guru set free

parts.note: a con is a convict

indicators.note: letters set free are released from their order and can fall into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A spiritual teacher is deemed fit to release a convict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set free' seems to release the prisoner, but it acts only on the letters of 'so guru'.
explanation.definitionFit: Congruous describes things in agreement or harmony, hence appropriate or fitting to the situation.

clue.text: Telltale wind energy moving from end to centre

indicators.note: going to the centre means it is put back inside the middle of the word
moving away from the end means a final letter leaves its place

parts.note: to wind is to snake, twisting along
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A gossip notices a wind vane shifting around.
explanation.walkthrough: The E for energy is already the last letter of the word for wind; it simply relocates into the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A sneak is the schoolyard term for one who tells tales on others to those in authority.

clue.text: Sticks best snapped to contain fever temperature

indicators.note: to contain is to hold within, so one piece sits inside the other
something snapped is broken, and broken letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
ague is an old word for a malarial fever
T is the abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: The best sticks are broken to stop a feverish temperature spreading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sticks' looks like the wooden kind being snapped; it is the definition, and only 'best' is broken up.
explanation.definitionFit: Long thin French loaves are called sticks of bread, the literal meaning of the French word.

clue.text: Female fish

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for female
the ling is a long sea fish of the cod family

explanation.walkthrough: With no definition, this looks like a hunt for a fish name; the answer is one of the preamble's set.
explanation.definitionFit: The Highland fling is a lively solo Scottish dance, so it belongs to the preamble's shared category.

clue.text: Select cure-all when heart skips

indicators.note: a skipped heartbeat is missing, so the middle part of the word drops out

parts.note: taken as written, hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: Choosing a universal remedy for an irregular heartbeat.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart removed is the three middle letters, leaving two at each end.
explanation.definitionFit: To cull is to pick out from a group, originally choosing animals for removal, so to choose.

clue.text: Dog died in town on south coast

indicators.note: being in a place means sitting inside it, enclosed by its letters

parts.note: Poole is a port town in Dorset on England's south coast
D is the abbreviation for died, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A sad news item about a dog that died in a seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: Poole is a harbour town in Dorset, on the south coast of England.
explanation.definitionFit: The poodle is a curly-coated breed of dog, so it is an example of the general term.

clue.text: This, tailored, goes outside to fit tight and good, like a hood

indicators.note: going outside means wrapping around, so these letters enclose others
a tailored garment is cut and remade to a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
clothes that hug the body fit tightly
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A tailored garment worn on top, snug and good, with a hood like a hoodie.
explanation.walkthrough: The tailoring vocabulary makes 'hood' look like part of a garment; it is short for hoodlum, a gangster.
explanation.definitionFit: A hood is slang for a hoodlum or gangster, and behaving like one is violent and brutish.

clue.text: Popular northern coach stop once?

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: A well-liked northern stopping place for coaches in bygone days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' today suggests a bus; the question mark and 'once' point to horse-drawn stagecoaches.
explanation.definitionFit: Stagecoaches historically halted at roadside hostelries to change horses and give travellers food and beds.

clue.text: People mentioned earlier, taking time out

indicators.note: taking something out means removing it from the word

parts.note: they is the pronoun for people already referred to
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: The people already named are having a break.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no definition: the answer is one of the preamble's set.
explanation.definitionFit: The hey, or hay, is an old English country dance in which performers weave in and out, matching the preamble's category.

clue.text: Stocking items of willow in outskirts of Henley

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, between its letters
the outskirts of a town are its edges, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the town's name
an osier is a willow used for basketwork

explanation.surface: A shop on the edge of Henley stocks goods made of willow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stocking' looks like a verb about a shop holding goods, but it is a noun: items such as stockings.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosiery is the trade term for socks, tights and stockings, the goods a hosier sells.

clue.text: Bear up without love

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top
without means lacking, so a letter is removed

parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh, the famous bear of A.A. Milne's stories
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Someone stays strong despite having no love in their life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear up' reads as one phrase meaning cope; split it, and the bear is Pooh, turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A hop is an informal dance party or step, as in a 1950s sock hop, fitting the preamble's shared category.

clue.text: Talk about what an old chest might do

definitions.text: what an old chest might do

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: gas is idle chatter

explanation.surface: A conversation about an antique storage chest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chest' suggests furniture, but it is an ageing body whose chest droops; the definition is a verb phrase, matching the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: With age, flesh and muscle lose firmness and droop downward, which is exactly to droop or sink.

clue.text: Pre-industrial housing check

indicators.note: housing means giving shelter inside, so the letters sit within the phrase

parts.note: inside the hyphenated word, spanning the hyphen

explanation.surface: An inspection of housing from before the factory age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing check' looks like a building inspection; 'housing' is the signal and 'check' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To check is to restrain or hold back, as a rider restrains a horse with the reins.

clue.text: Eloquence, force applied to production of Uncle Vanya, 4/5ths through

parts.note: F is the symbol for force

indicators.note: a stage production reworks its material into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: four-fifths of the way through a five-letter name lands on its fourth letter

parts.note: fourth of the five letters

explanation.surface: An actor brings eloquence and force to a staging of Chekhov's play, most of the way through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncle Vanya' reads as one title, but the two words do different jobs: one is fodder, the other supplies a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Eloquence is the gift of smooth, persuasive speech, which is having ready, flowing command of words.

clue.text: Former lines said by those people casually rising

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: ex means former and queues are lines of people

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading from the bottom up

parts.note: 'em is the casual form of them

explanation.surface: Old dialogue spoken by people in an informal, rebellious way.
explanation.walkthrough: No definition: the answer is one of the preamble's set.
explanation.definitionFit: An excuse-me is a ballroom dance in which someone may cut in and claim another's partner, fitting the preamble's category.

clue.text: Pulsating TV in for repair (underwear stuffed inside)

indicators.note: stuffed inside means packed into the middle of something else
something sent for repair is taken apart and put back together differently

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a bra is an item of underwear

explanation.surface: A flickering television is sent in to be fixed with a bra stuffed in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulsating' sounds like a fault on the TV screen, but it is the definition, in the sense of full of life.
explanation.definitionFit: Vibrant means throbbing with energy or vibrating, so lively and resonant like something that pulses.

clue.text: Scorer has space to turn, getting one in, then another one

indicators.note: turning round sends the letters back the opposite way

parts.note: a gap is a space
an means one
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A goalscorer finds room to turn, slots one in, and then another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scorer' reads as a footballer; it means someone who writes musical scores. Paganini was an Italian violinist and composer.
explanation.definitionFit: A composer writes scores, and Niccolò Paganini wrote famous violin works such as the Caprices.

clue.text: Noble, short winding stair ring

indicators.note: something winding twists and turns, so the letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a ring is shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A nobleman climbs a short spiral staircase in a ring-shaped tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' belongs to the definition, signalling an abbreviated word, not a letter to cut from the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the informal clipped form of aristocrat, a person of noble birth.

clue.text: Jolson and the Hobos LPs?

parts.note: Al Jolson, the American singer of The Jazz Singer
bum is American slang for a hobo or tramp

explanation.surface: Records by Al Jolson and a band called the Hobos.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a recording act's name; split it into a first name and a word for tramps.
explanation.definitionFit: LP stands for long-playing record, and such full-length vinyl records are what people call albums.

clue.text: Mate who makes a mess

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for a friend or pal
second meaning: one who mucks things up

explanation.surface: A friend who leaves everything untidy.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a mucker is a close friend, often in 'my old mucker'; literally, one who mucks about or mucks things up.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun works as informal British slang for a pal and as an agent noun from muck, meaning dirt.

clue.text: Cryptic crossword indication for "too pat"

parts.note: surface reading: asking which clue would lead a solver to the short phrase quoted
setter's reading: the answer is itself a complete anagram clue, a crushing word followed by six letters of fodder that rearrange into the quoted phrase

explanation.surface: A teaching question: how would a setter clue a glib phrase?
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer reads as an anagram signal plus fodder, and the vegetable shuffled gives TOOPAT.
explanation.definitionFit: The mashed potato was a popular 1960s novelty dance with twisting feet, so it belongs to the preamble's shared category.

clue.text: Sequined, unhemmed, like an Arab?

indicators.note: a hem is a garment's edge, so removing it strips off the outer letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sparkly robe without a hem, worn in Arabian style.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the Arab here is a horse breed, not a person in sequined dress.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arab, or Arabian, is a breed of horse, so it is horse-like by definition, an example.

clue.text: Breadth restricted by big car

indicators.note: being restricted by something means hemmed in by it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a limo is a large luxury car
B is the abbreviation for breadth

explanation.surface: The width of a road is limited by a huge car.
explanation.walkthrough: No definition here: the answer is one of the preamble's set.
explanation.definitionFit: The limbo is a Caribbean dance of bending backwards under a lowered bar, fitting the preamble's shared category.

clue.text: Released when undressing a virile journalist?

parts.note: the press is journalism collectively, here standing for one of its people
a stud is a virile, sexually active man

explanation.surface: A racy scene in which a manly reporter is stripped.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is read in reverse order: a virile man of the press is a stud of the press. The question mark flags that liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: This two-part metal snap fastener on clothing is popped apart whenever garments are taken off.

clue.text: Lots of money rejected (round million)

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters run the other way
going round something means enclosing it

parts.note: pots of money means lots of money
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: A huge sum turned down, about a million.
explanation.walkthrough: No definition: the answer is one of the preamble's set.
explanation.definitionFit: The stomp is a jazz dance with heavy stamping steps, so it belongs to the preamble's shared category.

clue.text: Don't do a full shift down the pit, sap!

definitions.text: Don't do a full shift down the pit
definitions.meaning: first meaning, playful: to mine less than one should
second meaning: to weaken gradually, as tunnelling under a wall weakens it

explanation.surface: A foreman scolds a lazy miner for skiving off, calling him a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sap' looks like an insult, a fool, but it is a verb meaning to weaken; a sap was originally a siege tunnel.
explanation.definitionFit: To sap is to erode strength or confidence gradually, like digging away foundations from below.
